content.title: Tornado warning: shelter decision
content.summary: A tornado warning is issued while your household is at home. Practice where to go, how to protect yourselves there, and what to do when the warning ends.
content.objective: Practice getting to the safest place at home during a tornado warning and protecting yourselves until it ends.

sources.label: National Weather Service — Tornado Safety: During
National Weather Service — Understand Tornado Alerts

sheltered_lowest_interior.text: You took everyone to a small interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows.

protected_from_debris.text: You covered heads and necks and put blankets over everyone.

recognized_official_source.text: You checked official updates before going outside.

needs_tornado_drill.text: Practice your household's tornado shelter routine together.

needs_contact_review.text: Agree on a short text your household sends after a storm.

needs_update_check.text: Wait for official updates before going outside after a storm.

nodes.title: A tornado warning for your area
nodes.body: Storms have been building all afternoon. A tornado warning is issued for your area. Your sturdy home has no basement. There is a small bathroom in the middle of the ground floor, and a bedroom with large windows upstairs.
nodes.prompt: Where do you take your household?

choices.label: The small bathroom in the middle of the ground floor
choices.consequence: Everyone is together in a small room with no windows, on the lowest floor.
choices.feedback: The National Weather Service says to move to an interior room on the lowest floor of a sturdy building and avoid windows.

choices.label: The upstairs bedroom, so you can watch the storm
choices.consequence: The room is on an upper floor, next to large windows.
choices.feedback: The National Weather Service says to go to the lowest floor and avoid windows. Ready.gov says to stay away from windows, doors, and outside walls.

choices.label: Step outside to see how close the storm is
choices.consequence: You are outdoors while the warning is in effect.
choices.feedback: A tornado warning means a tornado has been sighted or indicated by radar. The National Weather Service says to seek shelter inside a sturdy building immediately and move to an interior room on the lowest floor.

nodes.title: Waiting it out
nodes.body: Your household moves to the small bathroom on the ground floor. You can hear heavy wind and rain outside.

messages.text: Got the warning too. We're going to our shelter area here.

nodes.prompt: How do you protect yourselves while you wait?

choices.label: Cover your heads and necks with your arms and pull blankets over you
choices.consequence: Everyone has their head and neck covered, with blankets on top.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov says to protect yourself by covering your head or neck with your arms and putting materials such as blankets around or on top of you.

choices.label: Leave the door open so you can see the hallway window
choices.consequence: The open door leaves you facing a window down the hall.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov says to stay away from windows and to watch out for flying debris.

choices.label: Drive across town to a relative's house
choices.consequence: You would be on the road while the warning is in effect.
choices.feedback: The National Weather Service says being in a vehicle during a tornado is not safe. Your household is already in an interior room on the lowest floor, where the guidance says to be.

nodes.title: The warning ends
nodes.body: The tornado warning's end time has passed and the wind has eased. You don't know yet whether there is damage nearby, or whether more storms are coming.

choices.label: Check official updates before leaving the room
choices.consequence: You hear what local officials are saying about your area.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov says to pay attention to EAS, NOAA Weather Radio, and local authorities for updated information after a tornado.

choices.label: Go outside right away to look for damage
choices.consequence: You head outside before hearing any updates.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov says to pay attention to EAS, NOAA Weather Radio, and local authorities for updated information, and to stay clear of fallen power lines or broken utility lines.

choices.label: Call everyone in the family to check on them
choices.consequence: You spend the next few minutes on calls, one person at a time.
choices.feedback: Ready.gov says to save phone calls for emergencies and use text messaging or social media to communicate with family and friends.

outcomes.title: You walked through a tornado warning
outcomes.body: You practiced three moments: getting to a small interior room on the lowest floor, protecting heads and necks while you wait, and listening for official updates before going out. If you do go out, Ready.gov says to stay clear of fallen power lines or broken utility lines. The National Weather Service says a mobile home isn't safe in a tornado; if you live in one, know the closest sturdy shelter.
